Abstract
This standard covers all aspects of safety and health in the welding environment, emphasizing oxygen gas and arc weld- ing processes with some coverage given to resistance and high energy beam welding, brazing and soldering. It contains information on protection of personnel and the general area, ventilation, fire prevention and protection, and confined spaces. A significant section is devoted to precautionary information, showing examples, and an extensive bibliography is included.

Foreword
This foreword is not part of this standard but is included for informational purposes only.
The huge demands for production placed on the United States by World War II brought a tremendous expansion to the use of welding. In mid 1943, it was recognized that some type of code or standard was needed relating to safe practices for performing welding. Under the auspices of the American Standards Association, the standard was drafted and pub- lished in 1944. It was entitled American War Standard Z49.1, Safety in Electric and Gas Welding, and Cutting Operations.
Following the war, the standard was first revised in 1950. Subsequent revisions occurred in 1958, 1967, 1973, and 1983. Each updated the standard in accordance with changing technology and welding practices. The revisions up to and including 1973 were largely evolutionary and closely preserved the format of the original war standard.
In 1983, a major rewrite was undertaken to take proper account of the vast changes in welding which had occurred in the 40 years of the standard's existence and to clarify the somewhat patchwork presentation that had built up during the evo- lutionary revisions. The scope was redefined to address in greater detail the safety rules to be practiced by the welder and enforced by welding supervision and management. Provisions which had appeared in earlier editions, but which dealt more with building construction and piping installation over which the welder had little control, were deleted. The 1988, 1994, 1999, 2005, 2012, and 2021 revisions follow this same philosophy. Revisions are identified by a vertical line in the margin next to the text.

Under no circumstances shall water be used to extinguish a magnesium fire. At no time shall any one person work alone on this removal procedure. Another person shall always be present in the immediate area in case of an accidental fire.

Annex F (Informative)
A Brief History of Precautionary Information
This annex is not part of this standard but is included for informational purposes only.
The present format of Clause 9, Precautionary Information, was developed by the combined efforts of the American Welding Society (AWS) and the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA). In the 1970s some members of these organizations determined it would be beneficial if the Precautionary Labels, in Clause 8 of the 1967 edition of ANSI Z49.1, Safety in Welding and Cutting, were supplemented with additional precautions.
The 1967 label only addressed Fumes and gases hazardous to health. Other hazards, such as Electric Shock, Arc Rays, and Noise were of concern. Independently, AWS and NEMA Committees began to develop additional label information. Members of both organizations alerted each other of their own committee’s work. As a result, it was decided to form an AWS/NEMA Joint Committee on Precautionary Labels (ANJCOPL). After years of work by committee members, a consensus was reached. The new format was presented to American National Standards Institute (ANSI) for inclusion in Clause 9 of the 1983 edition of ANSI Z49.1, Safety in Welding and Cutting.
